subject: Art and Culture
sub_topic: Natural sites — Kaziranga, Manas, Sundarbans, Western Ghats

concepts.name: UNESCO World Heritage Site Designation Criteria for Natural Sites (OUV Framework)
key_dimensions: Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) — definition and the 4 natural criteria (vii, viii, ix, x) vs. 6 cultural criteria
Which specific criteria each Indian natural site satisfies — trap: Western Ghats satisfies ix & x but NOT vii or viii
Difference between 'nomination' and 'inscription' process — role of IUCN as advisory body for natural sites vs. ICOMOS for cultural
Integrity and Protection conditions required alongside OUV for inscription

concepts.name: Kaziranga National Park: Ecological Significance and Legal Protections
key_dimensions: UNESCO inscription year (1985) and specific OUV criteria met (ix and x) — trap: often confused with being inscribed only for rhinos
Status as Tiger Reserve (2006) under Project Tiger — making it both a WHS and a Tiger Reserve simultaneously
Location in Assam on Brahmaputra floodplain — significance of annual floods as ecological process (not just a threat)
Five-Toed species of Big Five: Indian one-horned rhinoceros, Royal Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, wild water buffalo, swamp deer (barasingha)

concepts.name: Indian One-Horned Rhinoceros: Conservation Status and Kaziranga's Role
key_dimensions: IUCN Red List status: 'Vulnerable' — trap: students often mark it as 'Endangered'
Kaziranga holds ~70% of world's total one-horned rhino population — making it a single-site dependency risk
Schedule I protection under Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 — highest legal protection in India
India Vision for Rhinos 2020 and the Indian Rhino Vision 2020 program — translocation to Manas and other parks

concepts.name: Manas National Park: UNESCO 'In Danger' Listing and Recovery
key_dimensions: UNESCO inscription year (1985) — same year as Kaziranga, but placed on 'In Danger' list in 1992 due to Bodo insurgency
Removed from 'In Danger' list in 2011 — making it a rare global success story of recovery; trap: some sources still cite it as endangered
Triple designation: UNESCO WHS + Tiger Reserve + Biosphere Reserve + Elephant Reserve — one of few sites with all four
Transboundary continuity with Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan — ecological corridor significance

concepts.name: UNESCO 'World Heritage in Danger' List: Criteria and Indian Context
key_dimensions: Conditions for inscription on Danger List: ascertained danger (specific, proven) vs. potential danger (possible, not yet proven)
Manas as the only Indian WHS to have been on and then removed from the Danger List — trap: some confuse this with Sundarbans
Management implications: State Party obligations, corrective measures, and reactive monitoring reports
Comparison with Delisting mechanism — only one site (Arabian Oryx Sanctuary, Oman) has been fully delisted

concepts.name: Sundarbans: Transboundary World Heritage and Mangrove Ecology
key_dimensions: India's Sundarbans inscribed in 1987 — separate from Bangladesh's Sundarbans WHS (1997); trap: they are two separate inscriptions, not one transboundary site
Largest mangrove delta in the world — formed by Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta system
UNESCO criteria met: ix (ongoing ecological processes) and x (biodiversity/threatened species) — Royal Bengal Tiger as flagship species
Climate change vulnerability: sea-level rise, cyclone frequency (Amphan 2020, Aila 2009) as both threat to OUV and policy concern

concepts.name: Sundarbans Tiger Reserve and Human-Wildlife Conflict Dynamics
key_dimensions: Only mangrove tiger habitat in the world — ecological uniqueness vs. other Tiger Reserves
Human-wildlife conflict: tiger attacks on fishermen and honey collectors (Mouli community) — livelihood vs. conservation tension
Sundarban Biosphere Reserve vs. Sundarban National Park vs. Sundarban Tiger Reserve — nested boundary trap for MCQs
Irrawaddy dolphins, Gangetic dolphins, saltwater crocodiles as co-flagship species — biodiversity beyond tigers

concepts.name: Western Ghats: Serial Nomination and Component Sites
key_dimensions: Inscribed in 2012 as a 'serial nomination' comprising 39 properties across 6 states — trap: it is NOT one contiguous park but a serial site
States covered: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra, Gujarat — trap: Gujarat is included, often missed
Criteria ix and x — recognized as one of world's 8 'hottest hotspots' of biological diversity
Gadgil Committee (2011) vs. Kasturirangan Committee (2013) — differing ESA boundary recommendations and political controversy

concepts.name: Western Ghats as a Biodiversity Hotspot: Endemism and Conservation
key_dimensions: Defined as biodiversity hotspot by Conservation International — criteria: >1500 endemic vascular plant species AND >70% habitat loss
High endemism levels: ~5000 flowering plant species, ~139 mammal species, ~508 bird species with significant endemic proportion
Ecologically Sensitive Areas (ESA) under Environment Protection Act 1986 — Kasturirangan report recommended 37% of Western Ghats as ESA
Overlap between WHS boundaries and ESA boundaries — source of ongoing litigation and state government resistance

concepts.name: Biosphere Reserves vs. National Parks vs. Tiger Reserves: Overlapping Designations
key_dimensions: Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO MAB Programme) is NOT a WHS — common trap: Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve overlaps with WHS components but they are distinct designations
Tiger Reserves under Project Tiger/NTCA can coexist with WHS — Kaziranga, Manas, Sundarbans are both
National Park = highest protection under WPA 1972 (no human activity); Biosphere Reserve allows buffer/transition zones with human use
Ramsar Sites overlap: Kaziranga is also a Ramsar Wetland — triple or quadruple designation sites as high-yield MCQ fodder

concepts.name: Project Tiger, NTCA and its Relationship with WHS Sites
key_dimensions: National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) established under WPA 1972 (amended 2006) — statutory body, not just a project
Tiger Reserves among Indian Natural WHS: Kaziranga (2006), Manas (1973 original, reorganized), Sundarbans — implications for dual management
Buffer zone concept in Tiger Reserves vs. WHS buffer zone — different legal and management meanings
Latest tiger census (2022): India holds ~75% of world's wild tiger population — connection to WHS site management success

concepts.name: Ramsar Convention and its Overlap with UNESCO WHS Natural Sites
key_dimensions: Kaziranga declared Ramsar Site in 2024 (recent addition) — trap: many study materials predate this designation
Sundarbans Ramsar Site (1992) — predates some WHS-related discussions, showing independent designation track
Ramsar criteria for 'Wetlands of International Importance' — 9 criteria vs. UNESCO's OUV criteria — conceptual distinction
Sites that are BOTH Ramsar and WHS — Loktak Lake (Ramsar but NOT WHS) as a trap comparison

concepts.name: Elephant Reserves and Asian Elephant Conservation in WHS Sites
key_dimensions: Project Elephant (1992) — Kaziranga and Manas both fall within elephant range; Nilgiris complex (Western Ghats) is India's largest elephant reserve
Asian Elephant IUCN status: 'Endangered' — trap: confused with African Elephant which has two species with different statuses
Human-elephant conflict in Western Ghats — crop raiding, corridor fragmentation as policy issue linking WHS conservation and tribal rights
Elephant corridors identified by Wildlife Trust of India cutting across WHS component sites in Western Ghats

concepts.name: Madhav Gadgil Report vs. Kasturirangan Report: Western Ghats Policy Controversy
key_dimensions: Gadgil Committee (Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel, 2011): recommended 64% of Western Ghats as ESA with three zones — rejected by states as too restrictive
Kasturirangan Committee (High Level Working Group, 2013): reduced ESA to 37% (~60,000 sq km) — more development-permissive
Key conflict: Tribal and local community rights (Forest Rights Act 2006) vs. conservation obligations under WHS and ESA frameworks
Current status: ESA notification still contested; Supreme Court interventions — shows gap between WHS inscription and ground-level implementation

concepts.name: Mangrove Ecosystems: Ecological Functions and Policy Frameworks
key_dimensions: Sundarbans as reference case: carbon sequestration (blue carbon), coastal protection, nursery habitat — ecosystem services beyond biodiversity
Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification 2019 — mangroves protected under CRZ-I (highest restriction); conflict with development near Sundarbans buffer
National Mangrove Committee under MoEFCC — India's mangrove cover according to State of Forest Report (SFR) 2021: ~4992 sq km
IUCN classification of mangrove ecosystems as 'Vulnerable Ecosystems' — linkage to WHS OUV for Sundarbans

concepts.name: Flood Ecology and Brahmaputra Dynamics: Kaziranga's Natural Processes
key_dimensions: Annual floods as a WHS-recognized ecological process under criterion ix — creates new grasslands, removes invasive species, shapes habitat
Highway NH 37 (now NH 715) bisecting Kaziranga — wildlife corridors to Karbi Anglong hills used during floods; road-kill controversy
Supreme Court intervention on highway speed limits and construction near Kaziranga — judicial conservation precedent
Climate change altering flood patterns — threat to the very ecological process that maintains Kaziranga's OUV

concepts.name: Comparison of India's Four Natural WHS: Criteria, Year, State, and Unique Features
key_dimensions: Year of inscription matrix: Kaziranga (1985), Manas (1985), Sundarbans (1987), Western Ghats (2012) — chronological trap in MCQs
State location trap: Kaziranga (Assam only), Manas (Assam only), Sundarbans (West Bengal only — Indian portion), Western Ghats (6 states)
OUV criteria comparison: Kaziranga (ix, x), Manas (ix, x), Sundarbans (ix, x), Western Ghats (ix, x) — all share same criteria, but reasons differ
Unique superlatives: Kaziranga (rhino density), Manas (recovery story), Sundarbans (largest mangrove), Western Ghats (serial nomination, hotspot)

concepts.name: Mixed Heritage Sites vs. Pure Natural Sites: India's Classification Trap
key_dimensions: India has NO mixed WHS (sites meeting both cultural and natural criteria) — trap: Khangchendzonga NP is listed under cultural AND natural criteria making it India's ONLY mixed site (inscribed 2016)
Khangchendzonga as the exception to the 'India's natural WHS' grouping — high-yield trap when UPSC asks about mixed sites
Criteria i-vi = cultural; vii-x = natural; a mixed site must meet at least one from each group
Implications for management: Mixed sites require coordination between ASI-type cultural bodies and forest/wildlife departments

concepts.name: Wildlife Protection Act 1972: Schedules and Protection Levels for WHS Flagship Species
key_dimensions: Schedule I species (absolute protection, highest penalty): One-horned rhino, Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, snow leopard — all found in Indian natural WHS
Schedule VI: Protection of specified plants — relevant for Western Ghats endemic flora; trap: students forget WPA covers plants too
Difference between Schedule I protection and CITES Appendix I — both apply to rhino and tiger but are independent international/domestic instruments
Compulsory acquisition of private land within WHS boundaries — powers under WPA vs. Land Acquisition Act — governance conflict

concepts.name: Climate Change Threats to Indian Natural WHS: Specific Vulnerabilities
key_dimensions: Sundarbans: Sea-level rise projecting loss of Sunderban islands (Lohachara already submerged) — direct OUV threat; UNESCO reactive monitoring triggered
Western Ghats: Altered monsoon patterns affecting endemic species dependent on precise rainfall regimes — phenological mismatch
Kaziranga: Intensified/altered flooding from glacial melt in Himalayan catchments of Brahmaputra — habitat instability beyond natural cycles
UNESCO's Policy Document on Climate Change and WHS (2023 update) — States Parties required to submit climate vulnerability assessments
